title: I Tried to Fool a Scientific Publisher With AI
gist: An author used free ChatGPT and Gemini, then the autonomous research system FARS, to produce fake and AI-conducted papers and submitted them to IEEE Access; both were caught (ghost citations, heavy reliance on preprints, figure artifacts). The piece argues AI slop is straining volunteer peer review and that automated research blurs the line of legitimate science.

themes.theme: Scale of AI slop in publishing

insights.claim: An estimated 57 percent of published academic articles showed detectable LLM influence by 2025, up from 12 percent in 2023, and only one in 40 papers with statistical evidence of AI use formally disclosed it.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: AI-assisted content is now the majority of the scholarly record; undisclosed use means true prevalence is understated.

insights.claim: Over 12 percent of Nature Communications reviews in 2025 were found to be completely AI-generated, and some estimates suggest hundreds of thousands of fake, often AI-generated publications are produced annually.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: Peer review itself is being contaminated by AI, undermining the last line of defense.

insights.claim: IEEE's research-integrity manager Amanda Sulicz warns AI slop is eroding trust in science and every scientific process built over centuries.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: Trust erosion creates demand for verification and provenance tooling.
insights.quote: AI slop is completely eroding trust in science

insights.claim: A novice using only free ChatGPT and Gemini produced a realistic-looking optical-solitons paper in about two dozen prompts by breaking it into sections and switching models, reframing refusals as 'hypothetical'.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: Guardrails on general LLMs are easily bypassed by task decomposition, so fabricated papers are cheap to produce.

insights.claim: IEEE Access's integrity checks caught the fake paper on hallucinated references: STM Integrity Hub flagged 12 and MolecularConnections could not validate 24, including a classic single author 'John Smith'.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: Reference-validity automation is currently an effective filter against naive LLM fakes; vendors in research integrity benefit.

insights.claim: Expert reviewers found the fake paper professionally written but with very dense math, excessive acronyms in the abstract and a couple of confidently stated debatable physics claims, while the managing editor said nothing seemed majorly scientifically wrong.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: Superficial plausibility means human reviewers without domain depth may miss fakes.

insights.claim: FARS, an agentic orchestration system from Singapore startup Analemma with four agents for ideation, planning, experiment and writing, produced a research proposal in 21 minutes and a submission-ready paper in 2 hours after a computational experiment ran overnight.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: End-to-end automated research collapses the cost and time of producing papers, raising submission volumes.
insights.locator: Round 2: Using an AI Science Engine

insights.claim: FARS created 166 papers in 417 hours, and Analemma was acquired by Baidu while the article was being reported, with the online FARS service discontinued.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: Large platform acquirers are absorbing automated-research startups, signaling strategic interest.

insights.claim: The FARS paper had real references but IEEE Access would have rejected it for a huge percentage of non-peer-reviewed preprint citations, and the editor spotted a nonsense 'lhewl' figure label and random dots in an AI 'brain' graphic.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: Automated checks missed figure artifacts; detection relies on human review and may not keep pace with better models.
insights.quote: One figure included a red line labeled with the nonsense term

insights.claim: AI Scientist and Autoscience Institute papers were accepted through double-blind peer review at the International Conference on Learning Representations in 2025, and the author expects the waves of automated research to build to a tsunami.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: Automated-research output at volume will overload existing review and publishing infrastructure.

insights.claim: Systems like AutoResearchClaw, AI Scientist-v2, Zochi, DeepScientist and LabClaw are extending automated research, with LabClaw linking to autonomous labs generating real-world data for tasks like drug discovery.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: Autonomous labs extend AI-driven discovery into physical domains such as drug discovery.

insights.claim: IEEE Access receives about 60,000 submissions a year, accepts around 20 percent (about 12,000), and reviewer invitations per article have risen 50 percent since 2018, showing volunteer reviewer capacity is stretched.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: Rising reviewer scarcity increases the value of automated triage and reviewer-matching tools.

insights.claim: Publish-or-perish culture is the kindling, paper mills the gasoline and AI the accelerant, in Ivan Oransky's framing; AI exposes long-standing weaknesses rather than creating a new problem.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: Fixes must address incentives, not only detection tools.
insights.quote: publish-or-perish has always been there as kindling, paper mills are the gasoline, and AI is the accelerant

insights.claim: IEEE's publishing ethics director Luigi Longobardi says detection tools built today may not work against tomorrow's AI-created papers, leaving peer reviewers as the last line of defense.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: Detection is an arms race, favoring provenance approaches over classifiers.
insights.quote: building a detection tool today may not be effective with the AI-created paper of tomorrow

insights.claim: Analemma's Xiwen Su argues the paper will give way to a living knowledge graph of well-scoped human and machine contributions, with automated systems doing reproducibility, statistical and novelty checks and humans judging whether research matters.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: If adopted, publishers' product shifts from papers to verified contributions and graphs.

insights.claim: IEEE Access editor Jenny Mahoney argues AI should not be banned, that tools already automate triage such as author checks, tortured phrases, duplicate submissions and reference validity, and that the key question is whether work can be trusted and reproduced.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: Publishers will invest in AI triage and semantic reviewer matching rather than restrictions.

insights.claim: Longobardi suggests provenance trust markers, such as integrating lab equipment with blockchain to record who produced data and when, while the Max Planck Institute sample IDs with QR codes and Southampton's electronic lab notebooks are early examples.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: Research provenance and lab-instrumentation data integrity is an emerging niche.
